\chapter{Good Night}
\label{ch:la-good-night}
\hlchaptermodality{30}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can wish someone a good night in Latin, and say why the wish takes the accusative case.}

Wish someone bonam noctem, and say why it is not bona nox — Latin wishes take the accusative.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bonam noctem]{bonam noctem — real grammar, not a real citation}

\label{lesson:LA-C30-bonam-noctem}



\begin{quote}
You already have \emph{bonus} (good) and \emph{nox} (night, last lesson). Put them together for \textquotedblleft{}good night\textquotedblright{} — but the case they end up in is the real lesson here.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: bonam noctem — why accusative, not nominative}]
\textbf{Bonam noctem} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{good night}\textquotedblright{} — but notice: \textbf{not} \emph{bona nox} (nominative). Latin wishes and exclamations conventionally use the \textbf{accusative} case — the same \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Accusative of Exclamation}\textquotedblright{} behind the genuinely attested \emph{Fēlīcem nātālem!} (\textquotedblleft{}happy birthday!,\textquotedblright{} short for \emph{tibi fēlīcem diem nātālem exoptō}, \textquotedblleft{}I wish you a happy birthday\textquotedblright{}). Grammatically, \emph{bonam noctem} is a compressed exclamation — something like \textquotedblleft{}{[}\textbf{I wish you}{]} a good night,\textquotedblright{} with the verb left unstated, the same kind of ellipsis you'd find in a letter opening like \textquotedblleft{}\emph{Cicero Atticō salūtem} {[}\emph{dīcit}{]}\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}Cicero sends greetings to Atticus\textquotedblright{}). The bare nominative \emph{bona nox} would work too (with an implied \textquotedblleft{}\emph{sit},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}may it be\textquotedblright{}), but the accusative is the more natural, idiomatic choice for a wish like this.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: Be honest: real grammar, not a real citation}]
Here's the careful part, matching the same honesty already applied to \emph{quōmodo tē habēs?}, \emph{nihil est}, and \emph{crās tē vidēbō}: the \textbf{accusative-of-wishing} principle itself is genuine, solid Classical Latin grammar. But this \textbf{specific fixed phrase}, \emph{bonam noctem}, is \textbf{not} actually attested as a Roman farewell formula in any surviving classical text — it appears to be a later, post-classical convention, built correctly from real grammar but not itself a citation. Treat the grammar as reliable and the exact phrase as a well-formed construction, not a quotation from a Roman text.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}

  \item \textquotedblleft{}bonam noctem\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}good night,\textquotedblright{} accusative
  \item the case rule — Latin wishes take the accusative, not the nominative \emph{bona nox}
  \item the honest caveat — solid grammar, but not itself an attested ancient farewell
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is it \textbf{bonam noctem} and not \textbf{bona nox}? (\textbf{Latin wishes/exclamations conventionally take the accusative case}, not the nominative.) Is the accusative-of-wishing rule itself solid Classical Latin grammar? (\textbf{Yes.}) Is \emph{bonam noctem} as one specific fixed phrase directly attested as a Roman farewell in any surviving classical text? (\textbf{No} — the grammar is real, but this exact phrase appears to be a later, post-classical convention.)
\end{tcolorbox}
